notes: Mandatory lifer parole review timing challenge; Article 5(4) analysis and declaration are clear despite some post-judgment corrections.

enrichment.short_title: Parole review interval and Article 5(4) for mandatory lifer
key_facts: Mr Day was sentenced to custody for life with an 11-year tariff after a murder committed when he was 19.
After tariff expiry in August 2003 the Parole Board refused release but recommended transfer to open conditions.
The Secretary of State fixed the next Parole Board review to conclude by August 2005, about 21–22 months after the last review.
The claimant challenged both the lawfulness of the Secretary of State fixing review dates and the particular interval as incompatible with Article 5(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision fixing the date of the claimant's next Parole Board review.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that postponing the review to August 2005 would violate the claimant's Article 5(4) right to a speedy review; claim that only the Parole Board may set review dates rejected; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: The Secretary of State may lawfully fix the timing of Parole Board reviews without infringing Article 5(4), but whether a chosen interval is 'speedy' is a question for the court on the facts, not a Wednesbury review; where a lifer is progressing well and rehabilitation work is short, an interval effectively approaching two years may fail Article 5(4) even if internal procedures allow earlier review requests.
legal_issues: Whether fixing the date of a Parole Board review must be a judicial function
Whether an interval of more than 12 months presumptively breaches Article 5(4)
Whether the Secretary of State's August 2005 review date was a speedy review in the circumstances
Whether the challenge was premature

notes: Teenage horseplay injury appeal; negligence and consent standards in informal play are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Negligence and consent in teenage horseplay injury
key_facts: Two 15-year-olds engaged in good-natured horseplay throwing bark chippings during a jazz quintet break in Devon.
The claimant threw bark at the defendant's lower body; the defendant threw it back, striking the claimant's eye.
Damages were agreed at £23,500; the county court found negligence and battery but reduced damages 50% for contributory negligence.
The Court of Appeal held there was no breach of duty and that implied consent covered the injury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Plymouth County Court on liability in negligence and battery arising from informal horseplay.
enrichment.ratio: Participants in informal horseplay owe each other a duty of care breached only by recklessness or a very high degree of carelessness; by joining the game a participant impliedly consents to being struck on any part of the body where objects are thrown in accordance with the tacit conventions of the play.
legal_issues: Whether the defendant breached the duty of care in informal horseplay
Whether volenti non fit injuria defeated the negligence claim
Whether the claimant consented to battery
The appropriate standard of care for unregulated play as opposed to organised sport

notes: Renewed permission application in Eritrean asylum appeal; narrow arguable error on personal factors is identified.

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal in Eritrean ELF asylum case
key_facts: The applicant is an Eritrean citizen who assisted his ELF-member father before fleeing after a raid in which his father was killed.
An adjudicator allowed his asylum appeal, but the Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversed that decision on country information grounds.
The applicant's low-level ELF involvement and credibility were accepted; risk on return was the central issue.
Keene LJ refused permission on the papers; Laws LJ granted permission on renewed application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring refusal of asylum.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on a narrow basis; appeal to be heard by a three-judge court.
enrichment.ratio: Where the IAT overturns a fully reasoned adjudicator's decision and adopts a materially different approach, it is arguable that it must explain what it made of personal factors that formed part of the adjudicator's reasoning, even if it was entitled to prefer the Secretary of State's country material.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT adequately addressed personal factors relied on by the adjudicator
Whether low-level ELF involvement exposed the applicant to real risk on return to Eritrea
Whether the IAT was compelled to adopt a different approach from the adjudicator
linked_authorities: Subesh v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 56

confidence.notes: Permission reasoning is clear but the judgment does not decide the merits of the asylum appeal.

notes: Jubilee Line injurious affection limitation appeal; estoppel and waiver arguments comprehensively rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Limitation and estoppel in Jubilee Line injurious affection claim
key_facts: Bridgestart owned the Hop Exchange above Jubilee Line tunnels acquired by London Underground in 1994.
Settlement cracking allegedly caused injurious affection; reference to the Lands Tribunal was made in October 2002, more than six years after entry.
LUL relied on section 9(1) Limitation Act 1980; Bridgestart argued estoppel by convention or waiver based on a December 1994 letter.
The letter said settlement damage claims would not be considered if received more than two years after the line opened.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Lands Tribunal decision that a compensation reference was statute-barred.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no estoppel by convention, equitable estoppel, or waiver established.
enrichment.ratio: A reference to the Lands Tribunal for disputed compulsory purchase compensation is an action to recover within section 9(1) of the Limitation Act 1980; continued negotiations and a concession about a two-year claims window do not communicate a shared assumption that a statutory limitation defence would not be relied on unless that is clearly established between the parties.
legal_issues: Whether injurious affection references are subject to the six-year limitation period
Whether LUL was estopped from relying on limitation by the December 1994 letter
Whether estoppel by convention arose from mutual unawareness of the limitation period
Whether continued negotiations amounted to waiver

notes: Short criminal appeal on section 116 calculation for extended sentences; statutory construction is decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Section 116 recall period for extended sentences
key_facts: The appellant received a 4-year custodial term plus 5-year extension for sexual offences in April 2000.
He was released early in December 2001 and committed assault occasioning ABH in October 2002.
The judge returned him to prison for 684 days plus 15 months consecutive for the new offence.
The appeal turned on whether section 116's maximum recall period includes only the custodial term or the whole extended sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence for breach of licence following a further offence during an extended sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Under sections 85, 116 and 117 of the Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000 read together, an extended sentence's term for section 116 purposes includes both the custodial term and the extension period; section 117(5) puts the matter beyond doubt.
legal_issues: Whether section 116 measures the recall period from custodial term expiry only
Whether section 117(5) extends the relevant date to include the extension period
Whether the judge miscalculated the maximum recall period
linked_authorities: R (Sim) v The Parole Board [2003] EWCA Civ 1845

confidence.notes: Single issue of statutory construction resolved clearly on conceded statutory text.

notes: Specimen count direction challenge in serial rape trial; judge's direction upheld as correct for the case.

enrichment.short_title: Specimen count direction in Birmingham rape trial
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of four rapes and two robberies against prostitutes in Birmingham in 2000–2001.
The indictment contained specimen counts alleging repeated offences that were not separately identifiable by date or place.
The trial judge directed that where incidents could not be identified separately, the jury could convict if sure an offence of the kind alleged occurred on some occasion.
Counsel below had not objected to the written direction prepared before final speeches.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following grant of leave on a specimen count direction point.
enrichment.ratio: Where repeated criminal acts lack identifying features, a specimen count conviction requires the jury to be sure there was an occasion when the defendant committed the offence alleged; where separate occasions are identifiable, conviction requires agreement on the particular occasion; the judge's direction correctly reflected that distinction for this case.
legal_issues: Whether the specimen count direction required jury unanimity as to the same occasion
When a Brown-type direction is required
Whether the direction was too general where offences were not factually distinguished

notes: Construction adjudication jurisdiction after repudiation; part 8 declarations refused on agreed issues.

enrichment.short_title: Adjudication jurisdiction after CCTV contract repudiation

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: MJ contracted with Connex companies to install CCTV at 50 stations under Phase 9 of a franchise project.
Works started without a signed contract; SE later suspended works and MJ accepted repudiation in November 2002.
In February 2002 MJ and South Central signed a letter limiting Phase 9 works to the SC franchise area.
MJ commenced adjudication in February 2004 seeking damages; Connex SE sought declarations denying jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on adjudication jurisdiction following acceptance of repudiation and a later SC settlement letter.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations refused; contract held in writing under section 107; adjudication right survived repudiation and the February 2002 agreement save to the extent SE was released from future access obligations and lost profit claims.
enrichment.ratio: A construction contract may be 'in writing' for section 107 purposes where tender documents and meeting minutes record acceptance; an adjudication clause survives discharge by acceptance of repudiation like an arbitration clause; a bilateral accord between one joint contractor and the contractor releasing substituted performance can discharge the other joint contractor from corresponding obligations.
legal_issues: Whether the Phase 9 contract was in writing within section 107
Whether the right to adjudicate survived acceptance of repudiation
Whether the 11 February 2002 agreement ended SE's adjudication rights
Whether the February 2004 adjudication notice was an abuse of process

notes: SFO section 2 notices versus CPR 31.22 collateral use; foreign fraud investigation balance upheld.

enrichment.short_title: SFO notice versus collateral use of disclosed documents
key_facts: Claimants sued Viktor Kozeny and related companies for fraudulent misrepresentation over Azerbaijan privatisation investments.
Defendants disclosed documents brought into England from abroad; the New York District Attorney requested UK assistance.
The SFO served section 2 notices on both parties' solicitors seeking copies of disclosed documents.
Moore-Bick J permitted the claimants' solicitor to comply and refused the defendants' application to block production.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against orders on applications concerning compliance with SFO section 2 notices and CPR 31.22 restrictions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Compliance with an SFO section 2 notice involves 'use' of disclosed documents for which CPR 31.22 permission may be required; section 3(3) of the 1987 Act does not override that rule; absent special injustice, the public interest in investigating serious or complex fraud and international co-operation outweighs the general interest in restricting collateral use, even where foreign defendants brought documents into the jurisdiction only for disclosure.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 31.22 restricts production of disclosed documents to the SFO
Whether section 3(3) of the 1987 Act overrides the collateral use rule
What constitutes a reasonable excuse under section 2(13)
How to balance civil disclosure policy against foreign criminal investigation

notes: Substitute mortgage after undue influence on earlier charges; Crowe v Ballard and Kempson v Ashbee applied.

enrichment.short_title: Voidable substitute mortgage after undue influence
key_facts: Mrs Tinsley granted all-monies second mortgages over the matrimonial home in 1988 and 1991 to secure her husband's business borrowing.
The judge found the earlier mortgages voidable for undue influence with constructive notice to Yorkshire Bank.
In 1994 the bank required a new mortgage over 113 London Road as a condition of releasing the Hillcrest charge during divorce-related conveyancing.
Mrs Tinsley signed the 1994 mortgage believing she would receive the new home free of mortgage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against possession order based on the 1994 mortgage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; possession order discharged; 1994 mortgage set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Where a lender with constructive notice of undue influence on earlier voidable mortgages requires discharge of those charges and a substitute mortgage on different property as a condition of consenting to a transaction, the substitute mortgage is inseparably connected with the earlier voidable security and is likewise voidable against the bank.
legal_issues: Whether voidability for undue influence on an earlier mortgage taints a later substitute mortgage
Whether constructive notice persists when the same lender takes a new charge on different property
Whether the 1994 transaction was an unconscionable bargain

notes: Landmark IVF consent appeal under HFE Act 1990; statutory construction and Articles 8 and 14 comprehensively resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Withdrawal of consent to use stored IVF embryos
key_facts: Natallie Evans and Howard Johnston created six frozen embryos after she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in October 2001.
Both signed HFEA consent forms for treatment together with a named partner; Mr Johnston withdrew consent after their relationship ended in 2002.
Without use of the stored embryos Ms Evans had no prospect of a genetically related child because her ovaries were removed.
She sought injunctions and human rights declarations; Wall J dismissed the claim and the Court of Appeal upheld him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against dismissal of claim for continued storage and use of embryos after withdrawal of the male partner's consent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Mr Johnston lawfully withdrew consent; Schedule 3 requirement for mutual consent to implantation is Convention-compatible.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 3 to the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990, treatment services must be provided to the woman and man together until implantation; an embryo is 'used' only when transferred to the woman; bilateral consent may be withdrawn until that point, and that scheme is a proportionate interference with the woman's Article 8 rights necessary to protect the man's equivalent rights.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'treatment together' in Schedule 3
When an embryo is 'used' so that consent cannot be withdrawn
Whether the consent regime breaches Article 8 or Article 14
Whether estoppel could prevent withdrawal of consent
